tier_reason: Artifact repo is public with benchmark drivers main-perf.cpp, main-built.cpp, main-fpp.cpp and RunAll.sh. The paper (Sec. 7.1) states GCC 10.3.0 and a Xeon Gold 6336Y, and the repo's CMakeLists.txt sets the flags (-Ofast -DNDEBUG, -march=native). Measured against plain Bloom, blocked Bloom and the cuckoo filter authors' own implementation.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Build time for n=0.94*2^28 (~252M) keys: the prefix filter is faster than every cuckoo filter configuration by more than 3.2x (abstract: 3.2-3.5x) and faster than the vector quotient filter (TwoChoicer) by 1.39-1.46x. Cuckoo filter insertions slow down more than 27x as load grows, so its build time is close to that of a plain Bloom filter BF-16[k=11]. Negative-query throughput is higher than CF-12 at every load up to 95% (+55%, +40% and +2.8% at 50%, 70% and 90% load). Positive queries at 100% load are 28-40% slower than CF-12-Flex and 46-60% slower than CF-12. The plain Bloom filter is the slowest filter for queries. The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, but its false-positive rate is 3-6x higher. Space is 11.55-12.13 bits/key at a 0.37-0.39% false-positive rate (Table 3).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0 on Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Sec. 7.1). The artifact repo's CMakeLists.txt builds the benchmark targets measure_perf, measure_built and measure_fpp with -Ofast -DNDEBUG, and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS is -march=native.
corrections.caveats: The paper's 52%/79% figure is the cuckoo filter's query-throughput lead over the vector quotient filter at high load. It is not a lead over the prefix filter, so the earlier record misattributed it. The prefix filter beats CF-12 on negative queries at every load up to 95%, but it trails cuckoo filters on positive queries at full load (by 28-60%). The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, at a much higher space and false-positive cost. The README requires an Intel CPU with AVX-512. All numbers come from single-threaded runs on one Ice Lake machine. The license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md, although GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION. The paper is PVLDB 15(7) 2022 (the arXiv version is the full version). There have been no commits since 2022-09-12.

notes: Tier A holds. The 1.39-1.46x, 3.2-3.5x and 27x figures are on the arXiv page. The record said the prefix filter was 52%/79% behind cuckoo on queries, but that figure is cuckoo versus the vector quotient filter, so claimed_speedup and caveats are rewritten from Sec. 7.3-7.4. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 50 stars, last commit 2022-09-12, abandoned) is correct.

tier_reason: Table 3 of the JEA 2020 paper matches the record exactly. The paper states GCC 8.1.0 -O3 -march=native on an i7-6700 (Skylake). The benchmark code is public in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc, which today also includes Xor8-singleheader and BinaryFuse8-singleheader entries. The binary fuse paper (arXiv 2201.01174) states GCC 10 -O3 -march=native on the same i7-6700 and uses the same harness.

corrections.claimed_speedup: This record covers both filters in FastFilter/xor_singleheader. (1) Xor filters, JEA 2020 (arXiv 1912.08258, Table 3, 25% of queried keys present): at 10M keys, Xor8 takes 23 ns/query at 9.8 bits/key, against Bloom12 at 40 ns (12.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo12 at 31 ns (12.8 bits/key). Xor16 takes 27 ns (19.7 bits/key), against Bloom16 at 48 ns (16.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo16 at 32 ns (17.0 bits/key). At 100M keys, Xor8 takes 32 ns, against Bloom12 at 58 ns and Cuckoo12 at 38 ns. (2) Binary fuse filters, JEA 2022 (arXiv 2201.01174): the 3-wise filter reaches about 9 bits/key (12.5% above the lower bound) and the 4-wise filter about 8.6 bits/key (7.5% above). Xor uses 9.84 bits/key (23% above) and Bloom at least 44% above. Construction is more than 2x faster than xor filters, and xor and cuckoo construction are both slower. The 3-wise query speed is on par with xor and faster than Bloom filters. The 4-wise query speed is similar to cuckoo filters. The binary fuse figures come only from plots; the paper has no table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Xor paper: GNU GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native, 64-bit Linux executable. Binary fuse paper: GCC 10, -O3, plus -march=native on x64.
corrections.hardware: Intel i7-6700 @ 3.4GHz (Skylake) with 8MiB L3, the primary platform in both papers. The binary fuse paper also uses a secondary AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen 2), which has a 25% error margin.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded membership-query time against space overhead for 10M and 100M random 64-bit keys, with 25% of queried keys present (fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc). The binary fuse paper adds construction time per key and bits/key across set sizes up to 100M keys.
corrections.caveats: This record covers both xor filters and binary fuse filters. The repo ships xorfilter.h and binaryfusefilter.h, and the README recommends binary fuse, which is smaller and faster to build than xor. Xor filter is itself a listed baseline in this category, so this entry's claim is measured against Bloom and cuckoo filters. The blocked Bloom filter is faster for queries (16 ns against Xor8's 23 ns at 10M keys) at 10.7 bits/key and about 0.94% false-positive probability. The 2020 paper found xor construction roughly half as fast as Bloom and cuckoo construction, and binary fuse removes most of that cost. The filters are static: no inserts after construction. The paper numbers were measured on the C++ implementations in fastfilter_cpp release 1.0, not on this C header, although the current harness can run the single-header code. All runs are single-threaded on one 2015-era Skylake CPU. The sample query-benchmark output in the README (98.765 ns/q, 0.123456 s) looks like placeholder text, not a measurement.

notes: Tier A confirmed. The JEA 2020 Table 3 numbers match the record exactly. I checked the binary fuse claims in arXiv 2201.01174 and folded them into claimed_speedup and caveats, as the orchestrator asked. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 432 stars, last commit 2026-09-21, active, not a fork) is correct, and the README lists the Databend, nDPI, InfiniFlow and Pebble production users.

tier_reason: This is an upgrade from B. The Experimental Setup paragraph of the arXiv full version states an AMD EPYC 7702 and clang++ 11.0 with -O3 -march=native. The benchmark code and scripts are public in lorenzhs/BuRR (Makefile bench target, scripts/) and lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp (benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc, ribbon-benchmark.sh). Table 2 measures BuRR against Bloom, blocked Bloom, cuckoo, xor and xor+.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Space overhead over the information-theoretic minimum (arXiv 2109.01892 Table 2, false-positive rate about 1%, r=7/8): Xor 23.0%, Xor+ 14.4%, blocked Bloom 45-52% and Cuckoo12 40-46%. Plain Bloom is at least 44% by construction (1.44*log2(1/f)). BuRR ranges from 0.06% to 1.4% depending on ribbon width (0.21-0.48% at w=64). Speed: in the 64-thread parallel workload, BuRR and homogeneous ribbon Pareto-dominate plain Bloom filters. In that workload, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 215/215 ns for positive/negative queries and 190 ns/key to construct, against Xor r=8 at 386/392 ns and 586 ns/key. Sequentially, the faster BuRR variants are 'only moderately slower than Bloom and Xor filters'. For example, at n=10^8, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 82/74 ns for positive/negative queries against Xor's 41/41 ns, and constructs at 115 against 159 ns/key. The README's rounded figures are overheads 'as low as 0.1%' and below 0.5% for speed-oriented configurations.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang++ 11.0 with -O3 -march=native on Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Experimental Setup). The BuRR Makefile bench target uses -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7702, 64 cores, 2.0 GHz base / 3.35 GHz boost, 1 TiB DDR4-3200
corrections.workload: Space overhead, construction time and positive/negative query time (ns/key). Sequential runs use n=10^6 and 10^8 keys, and a parallel run queries 1280 filters of 10^7 keys from 64 threads. False-positive rates are about 1%, 10% and 0.05%. BuRR is compared against Bloom, blocked Bloom, cuckoo, Morton, quotient, xor, xor+ and fuse filters in the lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp harness (SEA 2022 best paper; the arXiv version is the extended one).
corrections.caveats: The main win is space, not speed. Sequential query latency is about 2x that of xor filters, and the blocked Bloom filter is fastest overall at about 50% overhead. BuRR beats xor and plain Bloom on speed mainly in the heavily loaded parallel benchmark. BuRR is a static retrieval/AMQ structure: no inserts after build. The comparison harness lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp is a fork of pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp, last pushed 2021-09-11. The README's '~20%' xor and '~10%' xor+ overheads round the paper's measured 23% and 12.8-14.4%. Building needs git submodules (tlx, ips2ra, DySECT, pcg-cpp, rocksdb).
